PHASE 7 — PINTEREST AND REMOTE IMAGE IMPORT

You are working on our existing simulated-human-artist drawing application.

The previous six phases have been implemented. The application uses FastAPI, OpenCV, NumPy, a drawing planner, and a vanilla JavaScript Canvas playback engine.

Current baseline:

  • Backend: 44 passing tests

  • Frontend: 94 passing tests

  • Existing POST /api/sketch image-upload endpoint

  • DrawingPlan contract containing schemaVersion, dimensions, strokes, actions, and metadata

  • Upload limit: 20 MB

  • Decoded image limit: 40 million pixels

  • Hatch-stroke safety ceiling: 120,000

Objective

Allow users to start a drawing by pasting an image URL instead of uploading a local image.

The primary use case is Pinterest.

For example, a user copies a Pinterest Pin link, pastes it into our application, chooses a drawing duration, and clicks Start Drawing.

The application obtains the image, validates it, converts it into strokes, generates the artistic drawing plan, and animates the result using our existing playback engine.

1. Frontend interface

Add two image-input methods:

  • Upload Image — existing functionality

  • Paste Image Link — new functionality

The user should be able to switch between them.

The link input should accept:

  • Standard Pinterest Pin URLs

  • Pinterest short URLs such as pin.it links

  • Direct image URLs, including Pinterest image CDN links

  • Other safe, publicly accessible HTTPS image URLs

Add:

  • URL input field

  • Image preview where available

  • Clear loading indicators

  • Helpful error messages

  • A Start Drawing button

  • Existing drawing-duration selection

Preserve the existing drawing interface and styling.

The feature should feel integrated with the existing application, not like an unrelated second tool.

2. Backend API

Preserve the existing POST /api/sketch multipart-upload endpoint.

Add:

POST /api/sketch-url

Example request:

{
"url": "https://www.pinterest.com/pin/123456789/"
}

The response must use the same DrawingPlan contract as the upload endpoint.

Extract the shared processing workflow so uploads and remotely acquired images ultimately use the same image-to-drawing pipeline.

Do not duplicate image processing, stroke generation, planning, or serialization logic.

3. Remote image resolution

Implement a small, well-defined image-source resolver.

Responsibilities:

  1. Validate the supplied URL.

  2. Identify the URL type.

  3. Resolve Pinterest links where supported.

  4. Obtain the actual image bytes.

  5. Verify that the response contains a supported image.

  6. Pass those bytes into the existing drawing pipeline.

For direct image URLs, fetch the image through the backend.

For Pinterest Pin links, investigate the officially supported Pinterest integration options first.

Pinterest API access may require authentication and permissions. Do not assume the API can read every public Pin.

If a public Pin webpage exposes a usable image through standard metadata and accessing it is permitted, implement a narrowly scoped metadata fallback. Do not depend on brittle scraping, browser automation, private endpoints, or bypassing access controls.

Support Pinterest short-link redirects when they resolve to an allowed destination.

Do not promise that every Pinterest Pin will work. Explicitly reject unsupported video Pins, inaccessible Pins, private Pins, and Pins whose media cannot be resolved.

Where automatic resolution is unavailable, show a helpful message explaining that the user can use Pinterest's permitted Download Image option and upload the saved file instead.

Design this so future image providers can be added without rewriting the endpoint.

4. Security — critical

Remote URL fetching introduces server-side request forgery (SSRF) risks.

Do not implement a naive requests.get(user_url) or equivalent.

Apply:

  • HTTPS-only remote fetching

  • Strict URL parsing

  • No embedded URL credentials

  • Rejection of localhost, loopback, private, link-local, multicast, reserved, and cloud metadata addresses

  • IPv4 and IPv6 validation

  • DNS resolution validation and protection against DNS rebinding

  • Safe destination validation for every redirect

  • A small redirect limit

  • Connection and read timeouts

  • Bounded response streaming

  • Maximum 20 MB downloaded image

  • MIME type checks plus actual file-signature and image-decoding validation

  • Existing decoded-pixel safeguards

  • No forwarding user credentials or cookies

  • No bypassing remote authentication or access restrictions

Prefer a restricted set of explicitly supported hosts for the initial implementation. If arbitrary public image hosts are supported, use a network-fetch mechanism that cannot reconnect to unvalidated destinations.

Do not introduce a general-purpose public URL proxy.

Handle image decoder errors safely.

5. Preview

Ideally, the user should see the selected image before drawing starts.

Do not bypass validation by assigning arbitrary untrusted URLs directly to the preview.

Reuse the validated image-resolution mechanism where possible.

Avoid downloading and decoding the same remote image twice in immediate succession.

If temporary image caching is introduced, keep it bounded, short-lived, and local. Do not persist imported images by default.

6. Performance and concurrency

Do not block the FastAPI event loop with synchronous remote downloading.

Use appropriate asynchronous network I/O.

Inspect the existing synchronous OpenCV/planning workload and preserve its behavior. Do not silently introduce uncontrolled processing concurrency.

Make downloads cancellable where practical, and ensure failures release network resources.

Do not degrade existing upload performance.

7. Error handling

Provide distinguishable, user-friendly errors for:

  • Invalid URL

  • Unsupported URL scheme or destination

  • Pinterest media unavailable

  • Private or inaccessible Pinterest content

  • Unsupported video Pin

  • Remote server timeout

  • Remote server rejection

  • Unsupported image format

  • Oversized download

  • Excessive decoded dimensions

  • Image decoding failure

  • Sketch-processing failure

Never return an HTML traceback or leak internal server details to the user.

8. Tests

Preserve the existing backend and frontend test suites.

Add tests covering:

  • Valid direct-image URL

  • Valid Pinterest-style URL parsing

  • Valid short-link handling

  • Redirect rejection to unsafe destinations

  • Localhost SSRF rejection

  • Private IPv4 and IPv6 rejection

  • DNS rebinding protection

  • Oversized remote response

  • Unsupported content type

  • Non-image bytes with image MIME type

  • Timeout and network failure

  • Private or inaccessible Pin

  • Unsupported video Pin

  • Valid DrawingPlan generation from downloaded bytes

  • Existing upload functionality remaining unchanged

  • Frontend switching between upload and link input

  • Correct loading, preview, success, and error states

Mock external HTTP responses for deterministic tests. Do not rely on live Pinterest availability for automated tests.

9. Content rights

Use only images users are authorized to process. Do not interpret a public Pinterest link as proof of permission to reproduce or redistribute the image.

Do not add public sharing or redistribution features in this phase.

10. Engineering boundaries

  • Preserve the existing architecture.

  • Do not replace FastAPI.

  • Do not introduce React or another frontend framework.

  • Do not modify the artistic planner or rendering engine unnecessarily.

  • Do not add large dependencies without justification.

  • Keep source resolution separate from image analysis.

  • Preserve the existing API contract.

  • Make changes incrementally.

Acceptance criteria

A user should be able to:

  1. Open the drawing application.

  2. Select Paste Image Link.

  3. Paste a supported Pinterest Pin URL or direct image URL.

  4. Preview the selected image where supported.

  5. Choose drawing duration.

  6. Click Start Drawing.

  7. Watch the existing simulated human artist draw the imported image.

Existing file upload must continue working exactly as before.

Run the backend and frontend test suites.

Report actual test outcomes, unsupported Pinterest cases, architectural changes, and any configuration requirements.

Do not claim that Pinterest integration works universally unless it has been demonstrated.

Implement the feature now, using the existing codebase as your starting point.

One important consideration

Pinterest says that not all Pins are available for download, and viewing an image on Pinterest doesn't automatically grant reuse rights.

PHASE 8 — THE QUIET DIGITAL ATELIER

Immersive UI/UX redesign for ambient, long-duration drawing sessions

You are acting as a senior product designer, interaction designer, and frontend graphics engineer.

We have built a functional simulated-human-artist drawing application using:

  • FastAPI backend

  • OpenCV-based sketch generation

  • Artistic drawing planner

  • Natural pencil movement and pressure simulation

  • Vanilla JavaScript Canvas playback

  • Local image upload

  • Remote image links and Pinterest import

  • Drawing durations from 2 minutes to 4 hours

The application is working well.

We now need to rethink the user experience around its true purpose.

1. THE PRODUCT VISION

The user enjoys drawing and watching drawings develop but does not always have time to physically draw.

The application lets the user choose an image and watch a simulated pencil artist gradually bring it to life.

Consider this scenario:

The user selects a portrait, chooses a 3-hour drawing session, and starts the artist.

They then open a physical book and begin reading.

The drawing continues on their laptop or monitor.

Every so often, they raise their head and glance at the screen.

They see the artwork progressing naturally: the composition developing, shading deepening, and details emerging.

They return to their book without needing to operate the application.

The experience should feel like a quiet artist working beside them.

THIS IS THE PRIMARY DESIGN SCENARIO.

We are not building a productivity dashboard, image editor, analytics application, or conventional drawing program.

We are creating an ambient artistic experience.

Our guiding principle:

"Set the drawing in motion, then enjoy watching it come to life."

2. FIRST AUDIT THE EXISTING FRONTEND

Inspect the actual HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas rendering, and existing UI.

Identify:

  • The current screen layout

  • How users upload or paste images

  • How duration is selected

  • How playback is started and controlled

  • How the drawing is displayed

  • How progress and remaining time appear

  • Existing fullscreen behavior

  • Existing responsiveness

  • Canvas sizing and DPI behavior

  • Any clutter, unnecessary visual elements, or problematic interactions

Use the actual repository as the source of truth.

Then implement an incremental redesign. Preserve the working drawing engine.

3. VISUAL DIRECTION — A PRIVATE ART STUDIO

Create a refined, calm, immersive design.

Aesthetic:

  • Warm off-white drawing paper

  • Muted neutral surroundings

  • Subtle charcoal/graphite typography

  • Very restrained warm gray or sepia accents

  • Generous whitespace

  • Carefully balanced proportions

  • Soft, subtle surface depth

  • Elegant, unobtrusive controls

Avoid:

  • Generic SaaS dashboard styling

  • Bright gradients

  • Excessive glassmorphism

  • Neon colors

  • Large decorative cards

  • Cluttered navigation

  • Flashing UI indicators

  • Unnecessary animated backgrounds

  • Excessive icons or labels

  • Constant informational noise

The interface should look like a thoughtfully designed artistic instrument.

Use a coherent design system with CSS custom properties for colors, typography, spacing, surfaces, and interaction states.

Maintain accessibility and readable contrast.

4. DESIGN TWO CORE MODES

MODE A — SETUP STUDIO

This is where the user prepares a drawing session.

Provide a clean, attractive interface for:

  • Uploading a local image

  • Pasting a supported image URL or Pinterest link

  • Previewing the selected image

  • Choosing drawing duration

  • Starting the drawing

Use the existing input functionality and API integrations.

Make the controls intuitive and reduce unnecessary steps.

A user should be able to start a drawing without navigating multiple screens.

Do not overwhelm the user with settings.

MODE B — IMMERSIVE DRAWING STUDIO

This is the primary experience.

Once drawing begins, transition into a distraction-free layout.

The drawing canvas should occupy most of the available visual area.

Place the artwork on a warm paper surface with restrained surrounding chrome.

The artwork should be the dominant visual element.

No persistent debugging panels, upload forms, configuration settings, or sidebars.

The experience should remain beautiful and understandable even if the user never touches the mouse again.

5. DESIGN FOR GLANCEABILITY

The user may be reading a book several feet away.

They should understand drawing progress within 2 seconds of looking up.

Display:

  • Drawing progress percentage

  • Current artistic phase

  • Estimated time remaining

  • A subtle progress indicator

Example:

"Developing shadows · 42%"

"1h 24m remaining"

The artistic phase must come from actual drawing-plan information, not fictional status messages.

Progress should reflect the playback timeline. Do not misrepresent it as the percentage of the final picture that is visually complete.

Make text readable without turning it into a distracting dashboard.

Keep essential progress visible even when secondary controls are hidden.

6. AUTO-HIDING CONTROLS

During active drawing:

  • Keep playback controls minimal.

  • Hide secondary controls after a short period of user inactivity.

  • Reveal them on mouse movement, touch, or keyboard focus.

  • Never hide controls while keyboard focus is within them.

  • Ensure keyboard-only users can reach every action.

Core actions:

  • Pause / Resume

  • Replay

  • Fullscreen / Exit fullscreen

  • Return to setup or start a new drawing

Prevent accidental destructive actions.

Keep controls visually quiet.

Avoid intrusive overlays over the artwork.

7. FULLSCREEN AMBIENT MODE

Implement or polish a dedicated immersive fullscreen experience.

Requirements:

  • Drawing canvas occupies the available display appropriately.

  • Preserve image aspect ratio.

  • Avoid cropping the artwork.

  • Avoid stretching or distorting the pencil geometry.

  • Keep the artwork centered.

  • Keep progress information understated.

  • Allow controls to fade away when unused.

  • Support Escape and conventional fullscreen controls.

  • Retain alignment between the pencil sprite and graphite canvas.

Take special care with Canvas pixel dimensions versus CSS display dimensions.

Do not reset the drawing bitmap during fullscreen transitions or resizing.

Support high-DPI displays without unnecessarily increasing memory usage.

8. LONG-DURATION SESSION RELIABILITY

This is extremely important.

Users may run the drawing for 2, 3, or 4 hours.

Investigate and improve:

  • RequestAnimationFrame timing behavior

  • Browser tab visibility changes

  • Screen wake behavior

  • Accidental refreshes

  • Browser resizing

  • Fullscreen transitions

  • Long-duration timeline precision

  • Pause/resume behavior

  • Recovery after interruptions

Use the Screen Wake Lock API where available to optionally keep the display awake during active drawing.

Handle unsupported browsers and wake-lock rejection gracefully.

Request and reacquire a wake lock only when allowed by browser lifecycle and permissions.

Release the wake lock when appropriate.

Do not claim that a browser can prevent every operating-system suspension.

For session recovery, investigate using IndexedDB to preserve the current drawing plan and playback position.

DrawingPlan payloads can be large, including tens of megabytes, so do not store the full plan in localStorage.

If implementing IndexedDB recovery, include storage-error handling, bounded retention, and an explicit way to discard saved sessions.

Avoid duplicating large plan data unnecessarily.

Where practical, a user refreshing the page should have an opportunity to resume the drawing instead of losing the session.

Preserve the current timing semantics unless a change is explicitly justified.

9. SMOOTH AND BEAUTIFUL DRAWING DISPLAY

Refine the presentation without breaking artistic realism.

Focus on:

  • Correct Canvas scaling

  • Paper color and texture

  • Crisp line rendering

  • Natural pencil-tip visibility

  • Smooth progression

  • No flickering or layout shifts

  • Stable progress overlays

  • No accidental graphite redraw

Keep the existing graphite, pressure, stroke, and drawing behavior engines intact.

An optional subtle paper texture is acceptable if efficient and visually restrained.

Do not add decorative animations that compete with the drawing itself.

The pencil movement is already the main animation.

10. NO DISTRACTING NOTIFICATIONS

This application is intended to accompany quiet activities such as reading.

Therefore:

  • No intrusive notification banners

  • No unnecessary sound effects

  • No periodic popups

  • No blinking progress indicators

  • No automatic modal dialogs during drawing

  • No constant debug log activity visible to users

If optional sound is ever supported, it must be disabled by default.

Keep the user informed without demanding attention.

11. COMPLETION EXPERIENCE

When the drawing finishes:

  • Stop the pencil naturally.

  • Leave the finished artwork visible.
